chapterTitle: Connecting to an Oracle Database and Basic SELECT Statements
aiGenerationNote:

Then, walk through executing `SELECT * FROM employees;`, `SELECT first_name, salary FROM employees;`, `SELECT DISTINCT job_id FROM employees;`, and `SELECT first_name, salary * 12 AS "Annual Comp" FROM employees;`. Use a split-screen view with SQL Developer on the left and the query results on the right. Highlight common mistakes like forgetting `FROM` or misspellings and show the error messages. screens.title: Connecting to an Oracle Database and Basic SELECT Statements
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we open a first working session with an Oracle database and learn the core SELECT queries that let you read data. You will meet the common connection tools used in the Oracle world, understand the pieces of connection information you need, and practice the simplest queries to retrieve rows and columns. We'll also contrast quick inspection techniques with production-friendly query practices, show how to get unique values, compute simple arithmetic results inside queries, and make output readable using column aliases. This knowledge matters because retrieving the right data efficiently is the gateway to analysis, reporting, and application behavior. For example, you might use a graphical tool to explore tables during design, then port the same SELECT statements into a script run by the command-line tool for automation. Watch for common pitfalls: asking for every column when you only need two, or using DISTINCT without considering performance. By the end of this chapter you'll be comfortable connecting, running basic SELECT queries, and making their results clear to readers and downstream systems. As you proceed, ask yourself: what exact columns will answer my question, and how will I make those results stable if the schema changes?

Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

screens.title: How you will practice
screens.narratorSegment: Practice is crucial. You'll run a short activity that inspects the HR sample schema to compare broad inspection queries with targeted retrievals. Begin by opening a connection in your chosen client and run an exploration query that returns all columns to learn the dataset shape. Next, request specific columns to see how output narrows and performance typically improves. Use DISTINCT to identify unique job identifiers and compute a simple annual salary by multiplying the stored monthly salary — then alias the computed column so your report is clear. Each step demonstrates why explicit selection and clear labels make downstream reporting easier and reduce surprises when schemas change. A common mistake to watch for is forgetting the table name; almost every SELECT needs a FROM clause. Another trap is assuming DISTINCT on a single column will deduplicate across other columns; when multiple columns are listed, uniqueness is determined by the combination. As you try queries, pay attention to how results appear in both GUI and CLI tools and note any error messages so you can correct spelling or connection issues.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Practice Plan

Guided activity: Employee data retrieval

Follow these steps in SQL Developer or SQL*Plus to build confidence with connection and SELECT patterns.

1. Inspect all columns

Use a broad query to learn the table layout, then note column names and types before crafting targeted queries.

2. Select specific columns

Request only the columns you need for the report or script to avoid unnecessary data transfer.

3. Use DISTINCT and compute

Find unique job identifiers and compute annual salary by multiplying monthly salary by twelve, then alias the result for clarity.

Common Mistake

Forgetting the FROM clause or misspelling table names will produce errors; check messages in the client to correct object names or casing.

Pro Tip

Use the graphical schema browser to confirm column names before writing queries, especially when unsure about casing or quoted identifiers.

screens.title: Client Tools: SQL Developer and SQL*Plus
screens.narratorSegment: Client tools provide the interface through which you open a session and issue S Q L commands. Two common tools in Oracle environments are S Q L Developer and S Q L*Plus. S Q L Developer is a graphical integrated environment that helps you browse schemas, compose queries with visual assistance, and view results in a grid. It is particularly helpful when you are learning a schema, building queries interactively, or preparing reports. S Q L*Plus is a command-line utility included with Oracle clients. It is lightweight, script-friendly, and often used in automated workflows such as nightly jobs or quick remote connections. A concrete example: you might open S Q L Developer to explore the HR schema, click through the EMPLOYEES table to inspect column names, and then copy those names into a script that you run with S Q L*Plus in a scheduled task. A common misconception is that the S Q L language differs between these clients; it does not. The S Q L you write is the same, but error messages and formatting differ. S Q L Developer may show formatted error dialogs and clickable links to objects, while S Q L*Plus returns compact text errors suited to logs. Key takeaway: pick S Q L Developer for interactive analysis and S Q L*Plus for automation, but write portable S Q L so your statements work the same in both environments.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Client Tools
Definition

SQL Developer

A graphical IDE for composing queries, browsing objects, and viewing result grids. Helpful for exploration and building queries interactively.

When to use

Exploring unknown schemas, formatting reports, copying column lists.

GUI benefits

Clickable object trees and inline data preview.

Example

Open a connection to the sample HR schema, expand EMPLOYEES, and copy the column list to compose a focused SELECT.

Definition

SQL*Plus

A command-line client used for running scripts and automating tasks. Favored in CI, scheduled jobs, and quick remote access.

When to use

Scripting, automation, and environments where GUIs are not available.

CLI benefits

Simple output suitable for logs and pipeline parsing.

Scenario

After exploring columns in the GUI, paste a concise SELECT into a script and run it in SQL*Plus for scheduled report generation.

screens.title: Connection Essentials: Host, Port, Service, Credentials
screens.narratorSegment: A reliable connection requires four pieces of information: the server host or IP address, the listener port, the service name or SID, and valid user credentials. The host and port direct your client to the machine and listener process that accept database connections. The service name or SID identifies the specific database instance on that host; using the wrong service name will connect you to a different database or fail entirely. Credentials — a username and password — authenticate you and determine which schemas and privileges you can access. For example, connecting to a development instance often uses a host like the local machine or a cloud endpoint, port 1521 as the usual default, and the HR sample service name. A common misconception is that credentials alone are sufficient; they are not — the client must reach the right network endpoint and service. Another trap is assuming the listener always runs on port 1521; some environments use custom ports for security. When an attempt fails, check error messages: network errors point to host/port issues, while authentication errors indicate credential or account problems. Key takeaway: validate each connection piece independently — ping the host and port, confirm the service name, then verify credentials — so you troubleshoot efficiently.

keyIdea.title: Verify each connection piece
keyIdea.text: Host, port, service, and credentials are all required; check them individually when troubleshooting connection failures.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Connection Essentials
Process Flow

Open a session

Confirm network reachability, target service, and authentication to establish a working session.

1. Host & Port

The network address and listener port route your client to the database server. If unreachable, verify firewall and DNS.

2. Service name / SID

The service identifies the specific database instance. Using the wrong name connects you to the wrong dataset or fails the handshake.

3. Credentials

Username and password authenticate and determine what objects you can query after connecting.

Troubleshooting checklist
  • Ping host and confirm port is listening.
  • Confirm service name matches the intended database.
  • Check that credentials are valid and account is unlocked.
  • Inspect firewall and network restrictions for remote connections.
Example

If connection fails with a network error, test reachability first. If it connects but denies access, verify username and password.

screens.title: Opening a Session and Running Your First Queries
screens.narratorSegment: Once you've provided host, port, service name, and credentials, your client opens a session and you can run S Q L statements. The canonical first command when exploring a table is a broad retrieval that shows you column names and data types so you can plan focused queries. For example, beginners often ask for all columns to see everything during exploration; this is reasonable for small sample schemas. In practice, however, retrieving all columns can return unnecessary data and should be avoided for large tables. A concrete scenario: you open a session to the HR schema, run a broad retrieval to inspect the EMPLOYEES table layout, then identify first_name, last_name, and salary to craft a second query that returns only those fields. A common misconception is that the exploratory query is equivalent to production usage — it is not. Production queries should list only the required columns so that network and database resources are used efficiently and future schema changes are less likely to break dependent code. As you try commands, pay attention to client feedback: syntax errors, missing FROM messages, or permission denials help you correct mistakes quickly. Practice switching between exploration and focused retrievals to build a reliable workflow.

keyIdea.title: Explore then refine
keyIdea.text: Use a broad retrieval to learn table structure, then write focused SELECT statements for production and reporting.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › First Queries
Code Walkthrough
-- Exploration: use the asterisk to inspect the table shape
SELECT *
FROM employees;

-- Refine: request only the columns you need for reporting
SELECT first_name, last_name, salary
FROM employees;
Note: code above is for display. Run these statements in your client to observe results.
Why inspect first

Exploration helps you understand available columns and values before crafting efficient queries.

Example workflow

Explore with a broad retrieval, identify needed fields, and run a refined SELECT that lists those fields in the required order.

Key Takeaway

Use exploration to learn structure, then list specific columns to keep queries efficient and stable.

screens.title: SELECT * versus Selecting Individual Columns
screens.narratorSegment: Two common approaches to retrieve data are using the asterisk to return every column, or explicitly listing the columns you need. Using the asterisk is convenient for quick inspection and exploratory work because it returns the complete row without typing each name. However, in production and larger datasets this convenience becomes a liability: you may transfer more data than needed, reveal sensitive columns unintentionally, and create brittle code that breaks when new columns are added or column positions change. Explicitly listing columns is slightly more work but gives you control over output order, reduces network traffic, and makes dependencies explicit. For example, if a report needs only first name, last name, and salary, listing those columns ensures that adding a new column to the table will not change the report layout or add unexpected content. A common misconception is that SELECT all guarantees faster development; in fact, it can slow systems and make maintenance harder. Closing question to consider: when you inspect a table, which fields are truly required for your task, and which would you avoid returning by default?

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › SELECT Comparison
Asterisk

Quick inspection

The asterisk returns all columns and is useful when you need a fast view of table content and structure.

When it's OK

Small development tables or one-off exploration queries.

Pitfall

Can reveal unneeded columns and causes larger network payloads.

Explicit Columns

Precise and robust

Listing columns limits output, documents intent, and protects downstream consumers from unexpected schema changes.

When to prefer

Reports, APIs, and production queries where performance and stability matter.

Benefit

Explicit order in results and resilience to new columns being added.

Example

If only first name, last name, and salary are needed for a payroll report, request those columns explicitly to avoid including address or manager identifiers that are irrelevant.

Key Takeaway

Use the asterisk for quick exploration only; list specific columns for production and reporting.

screens.title: DISTINCT: Getting Unique Values
screens.narratorSegment: The DISTINCT keyword instructs the database to remove duplicate rows from the result set, returning only unique occurrences. When DISTINCT is applied to a single column, it returns the unique values present in that column. When applied to multiple columns, DISTINCT considers the combination of values across those columns — the database treats each unique tuple as a distinct row. For example, if you request unique department and job pairs, you will get each combination only once, even if the same job appears in multiple departments. A common misconception is thinking DISTINCT will deduplicate values across different columns independently; it does not. DISTINCT can be resource-intensive on very large datasets because the database must compare values across rows; applying DISTINCT to many columns increases the cost since it compares combinations. Use it judiciously when you need unique values for reporting or for feeding downstream processes. Key takeaway: DISTINCT is powerful for removing duplicates, but consider indexes or grouped queries for large tables if performance becomes a concern. DISTINCT: Getting Unique Values means use distinct to return unique values; when multiple columns are specified, uniqueness is based on the combined values across them.. In practical terms, how distinct determines uniqueness and when to apply it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › DISTINCT
Definition

DISTINCT removes duplicate rows

When you need unique values, DISTINCT filters out repeated rows so each returned value or tuple appears once.

Example

Request unique job identifiers to see the roles present in your employee table, or request department and job pairs to see unique combinations.

When to use

Reporting, lookup lists, and reducing duplicates for downstream processing.

Performance note

DISTINCT can be expensive on large tables, especially with many columns. Consider indexed columns or aggregation alternatives when needed.

Quick Contrast

DISTINCT on one column returns unique values for that column. DISTINCT on multiple columns returns unique combinations of those columns.

Key Takeaway

DISTINCT is for deduplication, but its scope depends on which columns you include; use it thoughtfully on large datasets.

screens.title: Arithmetic in SELECT and Assigning Aliases
screens.narratorSegment: S Q L allows arithmetic inside the SELECT clause so you can compute derived values as part of the query. Common operators include addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. A practical example is computing an annual salary from a stored monthly salary by multiplying the salary value by twelve. The result of such an expression will appear with an automatically generated header, which is often not human-friendly. Use a column alias to give that expression a meaningful name for reports and downstream consumption. If the alias includes spaces or special characters, enclose it in double quotes so the database accepts it. For instance, you might label the computed value as "Annual Salary" so the output column is self-explanatory. A common pitfall is performing division without guarding against zero; dividing by a column that contains zero will raise an error. Later you will learn how to use defensive functions to avoid division-by-zero errors. Key takeaway: compute derived values inline to reduce post-processing, and always give those results readable aliases so others can understand your output. Arithmetic in SELECT and Assigning Aliases means perform arithmetic expressions in select to derive values and use aliases, optionally quoted, to present clear column names.. In practical terms, compute derived columns and label them for clarity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Perform arithmetic expressions in SELECT to derive values and use aliases, optionally quoted, to present clear column names.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Arithmetic & Aliases
Code Walkthrough
-- Compute annual salary and assign a readable alias
SELECT first_name, last_name, salary * 12 AS "Annual Salary"
FROM employees;

-- If you omit AS, the expression still works but the column header is less descriptive.
Practice: try computing quarterly pay by multiplying salary by three and assign the alias "Quarterly Earnings".
Why alias?

Aliases improve readability and are useful for reports and downstream code that consumes query output.

Caution

Division by zero will raise an error. Guard divisors or use defensive functions in later lessons.

Key Takeaway

Use arithmetic to derive values and assign clear aliases so outputs are self-describing.

screens.title: Common Errors: Missing FROM, Misspellings, and Case
screens.narratorSegment: When learning S Q L, you will frequently encounter three common error categories: forgetting the FROM clause, misspelling table or column names, and confusion about object name casing. The FROM clause tells the database which table to read; omitting it makes the statement incomplete and the client will report a syntax error. Misspellings are easy to make — table and column names must match the database object names; if you are unsure, use the GUI schema browser or list available columns in the client. In Oracle, object names are often stored in uppercase unless created with double quotes, so an unquoted table name is usually safe in uppercase form. A concrete troubleshooting example: a query fails with an invalid identifier error. Check the spelling of the column, confirm it exists, and verify whether it was created with a quoted identifier which enforces case sensitivity. A common misconception is that S Q L keywords are case-sensitive; they are not. The closing tip is to read error messages carefully: network errors point to connection issues, syntax errors point to the S Q L text, and permission messages indicate privileges. Fix the specific cause, then re-run the query to confirm success.

keyIdea.text: Error messages guide you: missing FROM is a syntax error, misspells cause invalid identifier errors, and case-sensitive quoted names must match exactly.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Common Errors
Error Types
  • Missing FROM: A SELECT without a FROM is incomplete in most cases.
  • Misspelled names: Confirm table and column names in your schema browser.
  • Case and quoted names: Quoted identifiers are case-sensitive in Oracle.
Example

If you get an invalid identifier message, check spelling and whether the column was created with double quotes and mixed case.

Troubleshooting Steps
  1. Re-read the error message to identify the category.
  2. Inspect the SQL for a missing FROM or misplaced keyword.
  3. Confirm object names in the schema browser and adjust casing if quoted.
  4. Retry and observe the new client response.
Pro Tip

Use the GUI to copy exact object names into your SQL or run a metadata query to list columns to avoid spelling errors.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we open a first working session with an Oracle database and learn the core SELECT queries that let you read data. You will meet the common connection tools used in the Oracle world, understand the pieces of connection information you need, and practice the simplest queries to retrieve rows and columns. We'll also contrast quick inspection techniques with production-friendly query practices, show how to get unique values, compute simple arithmetic results inside queries, and make output readable using column aliases. This knowledge matters because retrieving the right data efficiently is the gateway to analysis, reporting, and application behavior. For example, you might use a graphical tool to explore tables during design, then port the same SELECT statements into a script run by the command-line tool for automation. Watch for common pitfalls: asking for every column when you only need two, or using DISTINCT without considering performance. By the end of this chapter you'll be comfortable connecting, running basic SELECT queries, and making their results clear to readers and downstream systems. As you proceed, ask yourself: what exact columns will answer my question, and how will I make those results stable if the schema changes?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to connect to an Oracle database using common tools, run simple SELECT queries to retrieve rows and columns, control which columns appear in result sets, and produce readable results with unique value filters and aliases. First, you will identify the differences between a graphical client and a command-line client and choose the appropriate tool for exploration or automation. Second, you will open a session using host, port, service name, and credentials so queries execute against the intended database. Third, you will write SELECT statements that either inspect all columns during exploration or request specific columns for reporting. Fourth, you will use DISTINCT to remove duplicate rows and perform simple arithmetic within SELECT expressions, giving those expressions friendly labels using aliases. These objectives matter because accurate retrieval and clear presentation of data are the foundation for analysis, debugging, and application logic. As you work, test queries in both a GUI and a CLI environment to see how results and error messages differ.

Practice is crucial. You'll run a short activity that inspects the HR sample schema to compare broad inspection queries with targeted retrievals. Begin by opening a connection in your chosen client and run an exploration query that returns all columns to learn the dataset shape. Next, request specific columns to see how output narrows and performance typically improves. Use DISTINCT to identify unique job identifiers and compute a simple annual salary by multiplying the stored monthly salary — then alias the computed column so your report is clear. Each step demonstrates why explicit selection and clear labels make downstream reporting easier and reduce surprises when schemas change. A common mistake to watch for is forgetting the table name; almost every SELECT needs a FROM clause. Another trap is assuming DISTINCT on a single column will deduplicate across other columns; when multiple columns are listed, uniqueness is determined by the combination. As you try queries, pay attention to how results appear in both GUI and CLI tools and note any error messages so you can correct spelling or connection issues.

Client tools provide the interface through which you open a session and issue S Q L commands. Two common tools in Oracle environments are S Q L Developer and S Q L*Plus. S Q L Developer is a graphical integrated environment that helps you browse schemas, compose queries with visual assistance, and view results in a grid. It is particularly helpful when you are learning a schema, building queries interactively, or preparing reports. S Q L*Plus is a command-line utility included with Oracle clients. It is lightweight, script-friendly, and often used in automated workflows such as nightly jobs or quick remote connections. A concrete example: you might open S Q L Developer to explore the HR schema, click through the EMPLOYEES table to inspect column names, and then copy those names into a script that you run with S Q L*Plus in a scheduled task. A common misconception is that the S Q L language differs between these clients; it does not. The S Q L you write is the same, but error messages and formatting differ. S Q L Developer may show formatted error dialogs and clickable links to objects, while S Q L*Plus returns compact text errors suited to logs. Key takeaway: pick S Q L Developer for interactive analysis and S Q L*Plus for automation, but write portable S Q L so your statements work the same in both environments.

A reliable connection requires four pieces of information: the server host or IP address, the listener port, the service name or SID, and valid user credentials. The host and port direct your client to the machine and listener process that accept database connections. The service name or SID identifies the specific database instance on that host; using the wrong service name will connect you to a different database or fail entirely. Credentials — a username and password — authenticate you and determine which schemas and privileges you can access. For example, connecting to a development instance often uses a host like the local machine or a cloud endpoint, port 1521 as the usual default, and the HR sample service name. A common misconception is that credentials alone are sufficient; they are not — the client must reach the right network endpoint and service. Another trap is assuming the listener always runs on port 1521; some environments use custom ports for security. When an attempt fails, check error messages: network errors point to host/port issues, while authentication errors indicate credential or account problems. Key takeaway: validate each connection piece independently — ping the host and port, confirm the service name, then verify credentials — so you troubleshoot efficiently.

Once you've provided host, port, service name, and credentials, your client opens a session and you can run S Q L statements. The canonical first command when exploring a table is a broad retrieval that shows you column names and data types so you can plan focused queries. For example, beginners often ask for all columns to see everything during exploration; this is reasonable for small sample schemas. In practice, however, retrieving all columns can return unnecessary data and should be avoided for large tables. A concrete scenario: you open a session to the HR schema, run a broad retrieval to inspect the EMPLOYEES table layout, then identify first_name, last_name, and salary to craft a second query that returns only those fields. A common misconception is that the exploratory query is equivalent to production usage — it is not. Production queries should list only the required columns so that network and database resources are used efficiently and future schema changes are less likely to break dependent code. As you try commands, pay attention to client feedback: syntax errors, missing FROM messages, or permission denials help you correct mistakes quickly. Practice switching between exploration and focused retrievals to build a reliable workflow.

Two common approaches to retrieve data are using the asterisk to return every column, or explicitly listing the columns you need. Using the asterisk is convenient for quick inspection and exploratory work because it returns the complete row without typing each name. However, in production and larger datasets this convenience becomes a liability: you may transfer more data than needed, reveal sensitive columns unintentionally, and create brittle code that breaks when new columns are added or column positions change. Explicitly listing columns is slightly more work but gives you control over output order, reduces network traffic, and makes dependencies explicit. For example, if a report needs only first name, last name, and salary, listing those columns ensures that adding a new column to the table will not change the report layout or add unexpected content. A common misconception is that SELECT all guarantees faster development; in fact, it can slow systems and make maintenance harder. Closing question to consider: when you inspect a table, which fields are truly required for your task, and which would you avoid returning by default?

The DISTINCT keyword instructs the database to remove duplicate rows from the result set, returning only unique occurrences. When DISTINCT is applied to a single column, it returns the unique values present in that column. When applied to multiple columns, DISTINCT considers the combination of values across those columns — the database treats each unique tuple as a distinct row. For example, if you request unique department and job pairs, you will get each combination only once, even if the same job appears in multiple departments. A common misconception is thinking DISTINCT will deduplicate values across different columns independently; it does not. DISTINCT can be resource-intensive on very large datasets because the database must compare values across rows; applying DISTINCT to many columns increases the cost since it compares combinations. Use it judiciously when you need unique values for reporting or for feeding downstream processes. Key takeaway: DISTINCT is powerful for removing duplicates, but consider indexes or grouped queries for large tables if performance becomes a concern. DISTINCT: Getting Unique Values means use distinct to return unique values; when multiple columns are specified, uniqueness is based on the combined values across them.. In practical terms, how distinct determines uniqueness and when to apply it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

S Q L allows arithmetic inside the SELECT clause so you can compute derived values as part of the query. Common operators include addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. A practical example is computing an annual salary from a stored monthly salary by multiplying the salary value by twelve. The result of such an expression will appear with an automatically generated header, which is often not human-friendly. Use a column alias to give that expression a meaningful name for reports and downstream consumption. If the alias includes spaces or special characters, enclose it in double quotes so the database accepts it. For instance, you might label the computed value as "Annual Salary" so the output column is self-explanatory. A common pitfall is performing division without guarding against zero; dividing by a column that contains zero will raise an error. Later you will learn how to use defensive functions to avoid division-by-zero errors. Key takeaway: compute derived values inline to reduce post-processing, and always give those results readable aliases so others can understand your output. Arithmetic in SELECT and Assigning Aliases means perform arithmetic expressions in select to derive values and use aliases, optionally quoted, to present clear column names.. In practical terms, compute derived columns and label them for clarity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When learning S Q L, you will frequently encounter three common error categories: forgetting the FROM clause, misspelling table or column names, and confusion about object name casing. The FROM clause tells the database which table to read; omitting it makes the statement incomplete and the client will report a syntax error. Misspellings are easy to make — table and column names must match the database object names; if you are unsure, use the GUI schema browser or list available columns in the client. In Oracle, object names are often stored in uppercase unless created with double quotes, so an unquoted table name is usually safe in uppercase form. A concrete troubleshooting example: a query fails with an invalid identifier error. Check the spelling of the column, confirm it exists, and verify whether it was created with a quoted identifier which enforces case sensitivity. A common misconception is that S Q L keywords are case-sensitive; they are not. The closing tip is to read error messages carefully: network errors point to connection issues, syntax errors point to the S Q L text, and permission messages indicate privileges. Fix the specific cause, then re-run the query to confirm success.
